hmmt-feb-2008-team2-01.title: Two cases
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-01.body: The claim says $\min(x,y)+z=\min(x+z,y+z)$. If $x\le y$, both sides equal $x+z$; if $x>y$, both equal $y+z$. (If $z=\infty$ both sides are $\infty$; if $x$ or $y$ is $\infty$ the same two-case check works with $\infty+z=\infty$.) ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-02.title: Use the definition
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-02.body: Here $z^n=nz$. Without loss of generality $x\le y$. Then $(x\oplus y)^n=(\min(x,y))^n=nx$, and $x^n\oplus y^n=\min(nx,ny)=nx$. (With $\infty$ the same holds: $n\cdot\infty=\infty$.) ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-03.title: Min of sums
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-03.body:
First, for any reals $u_i,v_i$: $\min_i(u_i+v_i)\ge\min_iu_i+\min_iv_i$ (if the left minimum is attained at $m$, then $u_m\ge\min u_i$ and $v_m\ge\min v_i$).

Now for finite $x,y$:
$$p\left(\tfrac{x+y}2\right)=\min_k\left(a_k+k\tfrac{x+y}2\right)=\frac12\min_k\big((a_k+kx)+(a_k+ky)\big)\ge\frac12\left(\min_k(a_k+kx)+\min_k(a_k+ky)\right)=\frac{p(x)+p(y)}2.$$
If $x$ or $y$ is $\infty$ then $\frac{x+y}2=\infty$ and $p(\infty)=a_0$ (every term with $k\ge1$ is $\infty$), while $p(t)\le a_0$ for every $t$ (the $k=0$ term), so $\frac{p(x)+p(y)}2\le a_0=p(\infty)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-04.title: Graph of p
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-04.body:
We have $p(x)=\min_{0\le k\le n}(a_k+kx)$: the lower envelope of the lines $y=a_k+kx$. So $p$ is continuous and piecewise linear with slopes in $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$, and by the previous problem it is concave, so its slope is non-increasing in $x$. Since $a_n\ne\infty$, for very negative $x$ the line $a_n+nx$ is the lowest, so the leftmost piece has slope $n$.

For $k=1,\dots,n$ let $r_k$ be the $x$-coordinate of the leftmost point to the right of which the slope of $p$ is less than $k$ (take $r_k=\infty$ if the slope never drops below $k$). Then $r_n\le r_{n-1}\le\cdots\le r_1$, and on $[r_{k+1},r_k]$ the slope of $p$ is $k$ (with $r_{n+1}=-\infty$, $r_0=\infty$).

Let $q(x)=a_n+\min(x,r_1)+\cdots+\min(x,r_n)$. Each $\min(x,r_k)$ has slope $1$ for $x<r_k$ and $0$ after, so on $[r_{k+1},r_k]$ the slope of $q$ is exactly $k$ as well, and $q$ is continuous. So $p$ and $q$ have the same slopes everywhere, hence differ by a constant. For $x<r_n$ we have $q(x)=a_n+nx=p(x)$. So $p=q$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-05.title: Find a collision
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-05.body: With $n=3$: $f(3)=3+j(0)=8$ and $f(1)=1+j(1)=8$. So $f(3)=f(1)$ and $f$ is not injective, hence not a permutation of $\mathbb Z$. (Two balls would land at time $8\equiv2\pmod3$.) ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-06.title: Use injectivity of f
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-06.body: Write $a_i=j(i)+i-b_in$ with $b_i\in\mathbb Z$. Then $f(i-b_in)=(i-b_in)+j(i)=a_i$ (since $\overline{i-b_in}=i$). The integers $i-b_in$ ($0\le i<n$) are pairwise distinct (they have distinct residues mod $n$), and $f$ is injective, so $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ are $n$ distinct integers. They all lie in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, hence form a permutation of it. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-07.title: Throws land on the next throw time
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-07.body:
Let $S=\{t:j(\bar t)>0\}$ be the set of times with an actual throw; $f$ fixes every $t\notin S$, so $f$ permutes $S$ with $f(t)>t$ for $t\in S$. A $1$-ball sequence has $\sum j=n$, in particular $S\neq\varnothing$ (period-$n$ set). For $t\in S$ let $s(t)$ be the next element of $S$ after $t$; since $f(t)\in S$ and $f(t)>t$, $f(t)\ge s(t)$, so $j(t)\ge s(t)-t$. Over one period the gaps $s(t)-t$ sum to exactly $n$, and $\sum j=n$, so $j(t)=s(t)-t$ for all $t\in S$: each throw lands at the next throw time.

Conversely, for any nonempty set $R$ of residues mod $n$, define $j(t)$ as the gap to the next element of $R$ (mod $n$) when $t\in R$ and $0$ otherwise; then $f$ is a permutation (it cyclically shifts $S$ and fixes the rest), the sum is $n$, so it has exactly $1$ ball. This is a bijection between $1$-ball sequences and nonempty subsets of $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, so the count is $2^n-1$.

**Answer: $2^n-1$**

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-08.title: Total arc length in a window
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-08.body:
Draw an arc from each $t$ to $f(t)$, of length $j(\bar t)$. Fix a large integer $M$ and consider the arcs whose left endpoint lies in $[0,Mn-1]$. Their total length is $M(j(0)+\cdots+j(n-1))$, since the window contains $M$ full periods.

Now group the arcs by orbit. A fixed point contributes nothing. Each of the $b$ infinite orbits is a bi-infinite increasing sequence $\cdots<t_{-1}<t_0<t_1<\cdots$ with consecutive gaps at most $J=\max j$; its arcs starting in $[0,Mn-1]$ form a chain from the first $t_k\ge0$ (so $t_k<J$) to the last $t_l\le Mn-1$ followed by the arc to $t_{l+1}\ge Mn$ ($t_{l+1}<Mn+J$). So its total length $t_{l+1}-t_k$ lies in $(Mn-J,Mn+J)$. Summing over the $b$ orbits,
$$b(Mn-J)\le M\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}j(i)\le b(Mn+J).$$
Dividing by $Mn$: $b\left(1-\frac J{Mn}\right)\le\frac1n\sum j(i)\le b\left(1+\frac J{Mn}\right)$, and letting $M\to\infty$ gives $b=\frac1n\sum j(i)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-09.title: An example
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-09.body: Take $210$: the average is $\frac{2+1+0}3=1$. But $f(0)=0+2=2$ and $f(1)=1+1=2$, so $f$ is not injective and $210$ is not a juggling sequence. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-10.title: Equal tangents
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-10.body:
Let $x=AE=AF$, $y=BD=BF$, $z=CD=CE$ (tangent lengths from a point to a circle). Then $a=y+z$, $b=x+z$, $c=x+y$. Solving: $x=\frac{b+c-a}2$, $y=\frac{a+c-b}2$, $z=\frac{a+b-c}2$.

**Answer: $AE=\frac{b+c-a}2$, $BF=\frac{a+c-b}2$, $CD=\frac{a+b-c}2$**

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-11.title: Ceva
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-11.body: By Ceva's theorem it suffices to show $\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=1$. By equal tangents $AF=AE$, $BD=BF$, $CD=CE$, so the product is $\frac{BF}{CE}\cdot\frac{CE}{AF}\cdot\frac{AF}{BF}=1$. ∎ (The common point is the Gergonne point.)

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-12.title: Midpoint of the arc
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-12.body: Let segment $AI$ meet the incircle at $A_1$. Since $AE=AF$ and $AI$ is the bisector of $\angle EAF$ (the perpendicular bisector of $EF$), $A_1E=A_1F$, so $\angle A_1FE=\angle A_1EF$. By the tangent-chord angle, $\angle AFA_1=\angle A_1EF$ (both subtend arc $FA_1$). Hence $\angle AFA_1=\angle A_1FE$, i.e. $FA_1$ bisects $\angle AFE$. Since $A_1$ also lies on the bisector $AI$ of $\angle EAF$, it is the incenter of $AEF$. It lies on the incircle. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-13.title: Arc midpoints
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-13.body:
By the previous problem $A_1,B_1,C_1$ are the midpoints of arcs $FE$, $DF$, $ED$ of the incircle (the arcs $FE$, $DF$, $ED$ that do not contain the third touch point). Using inscribed angles,
$$\angle DA_1C_1+\angle B_1C_1A_1=\tfrac12\angle DIC_1+\tfrac12(\angle B_1IF+\angle FIA_1)=\tfrac14(\angle EID+\angle DIF+\angle FIE)=\tfrac14\cdot360^\circ=90^\circ,$$
where we used that $C_1,B_1,A_1$ are midpoints of arcs, so $\angle DIC_1=\frac12\angle DIE$, $\angle B_1IF=\frac12\angle DIF$, $\angle FIA_1=\frac12\angle FIE$.

The lines $A_1D$ and $B_1C_1$ meet at a point $Q$, and in the triangle formed with $A_1$ and $C_1$ the angles at $A_1$ and $C_1$ sum to $90^\circ$, so the angle at $Q$ is $90^\circ$: $A_1D\perp B_1C_1$. So $A_1D$ is the altitude of $A_1B_1C_1$ from $A_1$. Similarly $B_1E$ and $C_1F$ are the altitudes from $B_1$ and $C_1$, and all three pass through the orthocenter. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-14.title: Equal tangents again
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-14.body:
Let the $A$-excircle touch $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ at $X',Y,Z$, with $Z$ on ray $AB$ beyond $B$ and $Y$ on ray $AC$ beyond $C$. Tangents from $A$ are equal, $AY=AZ$, so $AB+BZ=AC+CY$, and tangents from $B$ and $C$ give $BX'=BZ$, $CX'=CY$. Hence $BX'-CX'=BZ-CY=AC-AB$.

For the incircle, $AF=AE$ gives $BD-CD=BF-CE=(AB-AF)-(AC-AE)=AB-AC$, i.e. $CD-BD=AC-AB$. Therefore $BX'-CX'=CD-BD$. Adding $BX'+CX'=BC=BD+CD$ gives $2BX'=2CD$, so $BX'=CD=BX$ and $X'=X$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2008-team2-15.title: Homothety
hmmt-feb-2008-team2-15.body: The homothety centered at $A$ (positive ratio) that sends the incircle to the $A$-excircle sends the tangent line to the incircle at $T$, which is parallel to $BC$ (since $DT\perp BC$) and lies on the side of $A$, to a tangent line of the excircle parallel to $BC$ and farther from $A$. The excircle's tangent parallel to $BC$ that is nearest to $A$ is $BC$ itself, so the image of that tangent line is $BC$ and the image of $T$ is the touch point of the excircle with $BC$, namely $X$ (previous problem). A homothety centered at $A$ maps $T$ to a point on line $AT$, so $A,T,X$ are collinear. ∎
